en: Parivāra 21.
Pañcavagga 1. Kammavagga
There are four formal acts:
the act by means of announcement, the act by means of a motion, the act by means of a motion and one proclamation, and the act by means of a motion and three proclamations—
these are the four formal acts.
In how many ways do they fail?
These four kinds of legal acts fail in five ways:
either by way of the subject matter, or by way of the motion, or by way of the proclamation, or by way of the boundary, or by way of the assembly.
How do formal acts fail by way of their basis?
When a formal act that ought to be performed in the presence [of the accused] is performed in their absence, it is an illegitimate formal act that fails in its basis.
When a formal act that ought to be performed with interrogation is performed without interrogation, it is an illegitimate formal act that fails in its basis.
If one performs a legal procedure that ought to be done by confession without confession, it is a legal act lacking its basis and contrary to the Dhamma;
if one grants a verdict of past insanity to one who deserves a verdict of mindfulness, it is a legal act lacking its basis and contrary to the Dhamma;
if one performs a legal procedure of further penalty against one who deserves a verdict of past insanity, it is a legal act lacking its basis and contrary to the Dhamma.
If one performs a *tajjanīya-kamma* (act of censure) against one who deserves a *pāpiyasikā-kamma* (act of further penalty), it is a legal act that fails in its basis and is contrary to the Dhamma;
if one performs a *niyassa-kamma* (act of demotion) against one who deserves a *tajjanīya-kamma*, it is a legal act that fails in its basis and is contrary to the Dhamma;
if one performs a *pabbājanīya-kamma* (act of banishment) against one who deserves a *niyassa-kamma*, it is a legal act that fails in its basis and is contrary to the Dhamma.
To perform a procedure of reconciliation against one who deserves a procedure of banishment is an illegitimate legal act that fails in its basis;
to perform a procedure of suspension against one who deserves a procedure of reconciliation is an illegitimate legal act that fails in its basis;
to grant probation to one who deserves a procedure of suspension is an illegitimate legal act that fails in its basis.
To send back to the beginning one who deserves probation is an illegal act with a deficient basis;
to grant the trial period (mānatta) to one who deserves to be sent back to the beginning is an illegal act with a deficient basis;
to rehabilitate one who deserves the trial period is an illegal act with a deficient basis.
One who grants full ordination to one deserving rehabilitation performs an illegal act that is defective in its basis;
one who performs the Uposatha on a day other than the Uposatha day performs an illegal act that is defective in its basis;
one who performs the Pavāraṇā on a day other than the Pavāraṇā day performs an illegal act that is defective in its basis.
Thus, actions fail by way of their basis.
How do actions fail by way of the motion?
Actions fail by way of the motion in five ways:
If one misapprehends the subject matter, misapprehends the Saṅgha, misapprehends the individual, misapprehends the motion (*ñatti*),
or sets aside the motion afterwards— in these five ways, formal acts fail on account of the motion.
How do formal acts fail on account of the proclamation (*anussāvana*)?
Legal procedures fail due to the proclamation in five ways:
one does not refer to the matter, one does not refer to the Saṅgha, one does not refer to the individual, one omits the proclamation, or one proclaims at the wrong time—
it is through these five ways that legal procedures fail due to the proclamation.
How do formal acts fail because of the boundary?
Formal acts fail because of the boundary in eleven ways:
they demarcate a boundary that is too small; they demarcate a boundary that is too large; they demarcate a boundary with a broken marker...
He establishes a boundary; he establishes a boundary using a shadow as a marker; he establishes a boundary without a marker;
standing outside the boundary, he establishes a boundary; he establishes a boundary in a river; he establishes a boundary in the ocean; he establishes a boundary in a lake;
he causes one boundary to overlap another boundary; he causes one boundary to encompass another boundary.
In these eleven ways, formal acts fail because of the boundary.
How do formal acts fail because of the assembly?
Formal acts fail because of the assembly in twelve ways:
In a formal act to be performed by a quorum of four, as many bhikkhus as are entitled to participate have not arrived,
the consent of those entitled to give it has not been brought, and those present raise an objection; or, in a formal act to be performed by a quorum of four,
as many bhikkhus as are entitled to participate have arrived, the consent of those entitled to give it has not been brought, and those present raise an objection.
In a formal act (*kamma*) to be performed by a quorum of four, as many monks as are entitled to participate have arrived; the consent of those entitled to give their consent has been brought forth;
yet those present raise an objection.
In a formal act to be performed by a quorum of five … [and so on].
In a formal act performed by a group of ten ... [and so on] ...
in a formal act performed by a group of twenty: if as many bhikkhus as are entitled to participate in the act have not arrived;

if the consent of those entitled to give their consent has not been brought forward; if those present raise an objection; [and likewise] in a formal act performed by a group of twenty, as many [as are required]...
The monks eligible for the legal act have arrived; the consent of those entitled to give their consent has not been brought;
those present raise an objection. In a legal act requiring a quorum of twenty, the monks eligible for the legal act have arrived;
the consent of those entitled to give their consent has been brought; those present raise an objection.
In these twelve ways, formal acts (*kamma*) fail within an assembly.

In a formal act to be carried out by a quorum of four, there must be four regular monks (*pakatatta*) who are eligible for the act; the remaining regular monks are those entitled to give their consent (*chandāraha*).
The one for whom the Saṅgha performs the act is neither eligible for the act nor entitled to give consent, but rather is one who is the object of the act (*kammāraha*).

In a formal act (*kamma*) performed by a group of five, five bhikkhus who are regular members (*pakatatta*) are those entitled to participate in the act (*kammapatta*); the remaining regular members are those entitled to give their consent (*chandāraha*).
He for whom the Saṅgha performs the act is neither one entitled to participate in the act nor one entitled to give consent; rather, he is one entitled to the act itself (*kammāraha*).
In a formal act performed by a group of ten, ten bhikkhus who are regular members are those entitled to participate in the act; the remaining regular members are those entitled to give their consent.

He for whom the Saṅgha performs an act is neither one who has reached the point of the act (*kammapatta*) nor one entitled to give consent (*chandāraha*), but rather one who is subject to the act (*kammāraha*).
In an act performed by a group of twenty, twenty bhikkhus who are regular members (*pakatatta*) have reached the point of the act; the remaining regular members are entitled to give consent.
He for whom the Saṅgha performs an act is neither one who has reached the point of the act nor one entitled to give consent, but rather one who is subject to the act.
There are four kinds of formal acts:

a formal act consisting of a mere announcement, a formal act consisting of a motion, a formal act consisting of a motion and one proclamation, and a formal act consisting of a motion and three proclamations.
In how many ways do these four kinds of formal acts fail?
These four kinds of formal acts fail in five ways:
either through the basis, or through the motion, or through the proclamation, or through the boundary, or through the assembly.
How do formal acts fail through the basis?
If one ordains a paṇḍaka, it is an illegitimate legal act with a deficient basis.
If one ordains one who lives in the community by theft, it is an illegitimate legal act with a deficient basis.
If one ordains one who has gone over to another sect, it is an illegitimate legal act with a deficient basis.
To ordain one who is an animal is an illegitimate legal act that fails in its basis.
To ordain a matricide is an illegitimate legal act that fails in its basis.
To ordain a patricide is an illegitimate legal act that fails in its basis.
If one grants full ordination to a murderer of an arahant, it is an illegal act (adhammakamma) that fails in its basis (vatthuvipanna).
If one grants full ordination to a defiler of a bhikkhunī, it is an illegal act that fails in its basis.
If one grants full ordination to a schismatic of the Saṅgha, it is an illegal act that fails in its basis.
If one ordains a person who has caused the appearance of blood, it is an illegal act that fails in its basis.
If one ordains a person with both sexual organs, it is an illegal act that fails in its basis.
If one ordains a person less than twenty years of age, it is an illegal act that fails in its basis.
In this way, formal acts fail due to their basis.
How do formal acts fail due to the motion?
Formal acts fail due to the motion in five ways.
One does not misapprehend the subject matter; one does not misapprehend the Saṅgha; one does not misapprehend the individual; one does not misapprehend the motion (*ñatti*);
or one sets aside the motion afterwards—in these five ways, formal acts (*kamma*) fail because of the motion.
How do formal acts fail because of the proclamation (*anussāvana*)?
Legal procedures fail due to the proclamation in five ways:
one does not refer to the matter, one does not refer to the Saṅgha, one does not refer to the individual, one omits the proclamation, or one proclaims at the wrong time.
Legal procedures fail due to the proclamation in these five ways.
How do formal acts fail because of the boundary?
Formal acts fail because of the boundary in eleven ways:
one establishes a boundary that is too small; one establishes a boundary that is too large; one establishes a boundary with a broken mark...
He establishes a boundary; he establishes a boundary marked by shade; he establishes a boundary without a mark;
standing outside the boundary, he establishes a boundary; he establishes a boundary in a river; he establishes a boundary in the ocean; he establishes a boundary in a lake;
he overlaps one boundary with another boundary; he encloses one boundary within another boundary.
In these eleven ways, formal acts fail because of the boundary.
How do formal acts fail because of the assembly?
Formal acts fail because of the assembly in twelve ways:
In a formal act requiring a quorum of four, as many bhikkhus as are entitled to participate have not arrived; the consent of those entitled to give it has not been brought;
and those present raise an objection. In a formal act requiring a quorum of four, as many bhikkhus as are entitled to participate have arrived;
the consent of those entitled to give it has not been brought; and those present raise an objection.
In a formal act requiring a quorum of four, as many bhikkhus as are entitled to participate have arrived, the consent of those entitled to give their consent has been brought,
and those present raise an objection.
In a formal act requiring a quorum of five … [and so on].
In a formal act performed by a group of ten... [and so on] ...in a formal act performed by a group of twenty:

if as many bhikkhus as are entitled to participate in the act have not arrived; if the consent of those who are entitled to give their consent has not been brought; and if those present raise an objection. In a formal act performed by a group of twenty:
if as many bhikkhus as are entitled to participate in the act have arrived; and if the consent of those who are entitled to give their consent...

The consent has not been brought; those present protest. In a formal act requiring a quorum of twenty, as many bhikkhus as are entitled to participate have arrived, the consent of those entitled to give it has been brought, and those present protest—in these twelve ways formal acts fail for the assembly.
To how many matters does a *apalokana-kamma* apply?
To how many matters does a *ñatti-kamma* apply?
To how many matters does a *ñattidutiyakamma* apply?
To how many points does a formal act consisting of a motion followed by a fourth resolution (ñatticatutthakamma) apply?
A formal act consisting of a mere announcement (apalokanakamma) applies to five points.
A formal act consisting of a motion (ñattikamma) applies to nine points.
A formal act consisting of a motion followed by one proclamation (ñattidutiyakamma) proceeds to seven grounds.
A formal act consisting of a motion followed by three proclamations (ñatticatutthakamma) proceeds to seven grounds.
To which five grounds does a formal act consisting of a mere announcement (apalokanakamma) proceed?
Rehabilitation, banishment, shaving the head, the Brahma-punishment, and the formal act as the fifth—these five points pertain to a formal act by way of notification (*apalokanakamma*).
To how many points does a formal act consisting of a motion (*ñattikamma*) pertain? It pertains to nine points.
Reinstatement, sending away, the Uposatha, the Pavāraṇā, formal consent, giving, receiving, postponement, and the characteristics of a legal act as the ninth—
these nine points fall under a legal act consisting of a motion.
What seven points does a legal act consisting of a motion and a second resolution fall under?
Reinstatement, sending away, formal authorization, giving, rescinding, confession, and the characteristic of a formal act as the seventh—
these seven points pertain to a formal act consisting of a motion and a second resolution (*ñattidutiyakamma*).
What seven points pertain to a formal act consisting of a motion and a fourth resolution (*ñatticatutthakamma*)?
Reinstatement, sending away, formal agreement, giving, censure, formal admonition, and the characteristic of the legal act as the seventh:
the legal act consisting of a motion followed by a fourth resolution proceeds through these seven points.

In a legal act to be performed by a quorum of four, there must be four regular monks who are entitled to participate in the act; the remainder of the regular monks are those entitled to give their consent.

He for whom the Saṅgha performs a formal act (kamma) is neither one who has reached the point of the act (kammapatta) nor one entitled to give consent (chandāraha), but rather one who is subject to the act (kammāraha).
In a formal act performed by a group of five, five bhikkhus who are regular members (pakatatta) have reached the point of the act; the remaining regular members are entitled to give consent.
He for whom the Saṅgha performs a formal act is neither one who has reached the point of the act nor one entitled to give consent, but rather one who is subject to the act.

In a formal act (*kamma*) performed by a group of ten, ten regular monks (*pakatatta*) are eligible for the act (*kammapatta*); the remaining regular monks are entitled to give their consent (*chandāraha*).
He for whom the Saṅgha performs the act is neither eligible for the act nor entitled to give consent; rather, he is one who is subject to the act (*kammāraha*).
In a formal act performed by a group of twenty, twenty regular monks are eligible for the act; the remaining regular monks are entitled to give their consent.
The one against whom the Saṅgha performs an act is neither subject to that act nor entitled to give consent; however, he is subject to the act.
The first section on the Act is finished.
2. The Section on Purpose.
The Tathāgata has laid down the training rule for his disciples based on two purposes:
for the well-being of the Saṅgha and for the comfort of the Saṅgha.
It is based on these two purposes that the Tathāgata has laid down the training rule for his disciples.
The Tathāgata has laid down the training rule for his disciples based on two purposes:
for the restraint of persons who are difficult to correct, and for the comfortable dwelling of well-behaved bhikkhus.
It is based on these two purposes that the Tathāgata has laid down the training rule for his disciples.
The Tathāgata has laid down the training rule for his disciples based on two purposes:
for the restraint of the taints pertaining to the present life, and for the warding off of the taints pertaining to future lives.
It is based on these two purposes that the Tathāgata has laid down the training rule for his disciples.
The Tathāgata has laid down the training rules for his disciples based on two purposes:
for the restraint of dangers pertaining to the present life, and for the warding off of dangers pertaining to future lives.
It is based on these two purposes that the Tathāgata has laid down the training rules for his disciples.
The Tathāgata has laid down the training rule for his disciples based on two purposes:
for the restraint of faults pertaining to the present life, and for the warding off of faults pertaining to future lives—
it is based on these two purposes that the Tathāgata has laid down the training rule for his disciples.
The Tathāgata has laid down the training rules for his disciples based on two purposes:
for the restraint of fears pertaining to the present life, and for the warding off of fears pertaining to future lives.
It is based on these two purposes that the Tathāgata has laid down the training rules for his disciples.
The Tathāgata has laid down the training rule for his disciples based on two purposes:
for the restraint of unwholesome states pertaining to the present life, and for the warding off of unwholesome states pertaining to future lives.
It is based on these two purposes that the Tathāgata has laid down the training rule for his disciples.
The Tathāgata has laid down the training rules for his disciples based on two purposes:
out of compassion for householders, and to cut off the faction of those with evil desires.
It is based on these two purposes that the Tathāgata has laid down the training rules for his disciples.
The Tathāgata has laid down the training rule for his disciples based on two purposes:
for the inspiration of those without confidence, and for the increase of those already confident.
It is based on these two purposes that the Tathāgata has laid down the training rule for his disciples.
The Tathāgata has laid down the training rule for his disciples based on two purposes:
for the endurance of the true Dhamma and for the support of the discipline.
It is based on these two purposes that the Tathāgata has laid down the training rule for his disciples.
The second chapter on the Benefits is finished.
3. The Chapter on What Has Been Laid Down.
The Tathāgata has laid down the Pātimokkha for his disciples based on two purposes... [etc. ...pe... [as before] ...pe... [end].
The recitation of the Pātimokkha has been prescribed;
the suspension of the Pātimokkha has been prescribed;
the invitation ceremony (pavāraṇā) has been prescribed.
The suspension of the invitation ceremony (pavāraṇā) has been prescribed;
the act of censure (tajjanīya-kamma) has been prescribed;
the act of demotion (niyassa-kamma) has been prescribed.
The formal act of banishment has been prescribed;
the formal act of reconciliation has been prescribed;
the formal act of suspension has been prescribed.
The granting of probation was prescribed;
the sending back to the beginning was prescribed;
the granting of the trial period (mānatta) was prescribed.
The act of rehabilitation has been prescribed;
the act of reinstatement has been prescribed;
the act of banishment has been prescribed.
The full ordination has been prescribed;
the act of obtaining permission has been prescribed;
the formal act consisting of a motion has been prescribed.
The formal act consisting of a motion and a second resolution has been prescribed... the formal act consisting of a motion and a fourth resolution has been prescribed... [and so on].
The third chapter on Prescriptions is finished.
4. The Chapter on What Was Not Laid Down and What Was Laid Down …pe… What was laid down when not yet laid down, and what was further laid down when already laid down …pe…
The resolution face-to-face has been laid down …pe… the resolution through recollection has been laid down …pe… the resolution for one who is no longer deluded has been laid down …pe…
The procedure of acting according to what has been admitted was laid down...
the majority decision was laid down...
the procedure of further penalty was laid down... [and so on].
The "covering over as with grass" has been prescribed by the Tathāgata for the well-being of the Saṅgha and for the comfort of the Saṅgha—
it is for these two purposes that the Tathāgata has prescribed the "covering over as with grass" for his disciples.
It is for these two purposes that the Tathāgata has prescribed the "covering over as with grass" for his disciples.
For the restraint of persons who are difficult to correct, and for the comfortable dwelling of well-behaved bhikkhus—
it was with these two purposes in mind that the Tathāgata prescribed the "covering over as with grass" for his disciples.
It was with two purposes in mind that the Tathāgata prescribed the "covering over as with grass" for his disciples.
For the restraint of taints pertaining to the present life, and for the warding off of taints pertaining to future lives—
it is with these two purposes in mind that the Tathāgata has prescribed the "covering over as with grass" for his disciples.
It is with these two purposes in mind that the Tathāgata has prescribed the "covering over as with grass" for his disciples.
For the restraint of hostilities pertaining to the present life, and for the warding off of hostilities pertaining to future lives—
it is with these two purposes in mind that the Tathāgata has prescribed the "covering over as with grass" for his disciples.
It is with these two purposes in mind that the Tathāgata has prescribed the "covering over as with grass" for his disciples.
For the restraint of faults pertaining to the present life and for the warding off of faults pertaining to future lives—
it is for these two purposes that the Tathāgata has prescribed the "covering over with grass" (tiṇavatthāraka) for his disciples.
It is for these two purposes that the Tathāgata has prescribed the "covering over with grass" for his disciples.
For the restraint of fears pertaining to the present life, and for the warding off of fears pertaining to future lives—
it is with these two purposes in mind that the Tathāgata has prescribed the "covering over as with grass" for his disciples.
It is with these two purposes in mind that the Tathāgata has prescribed the "covering over as with grass" for his disciples.
For the restraint of unwholesome states pertaining to the present life, and for the warding off of unwholesome states pertaining to future lives—
it is with these two purposes in mind that the Tathāgata has prescribed the "covering over as with grass" for his disciples.
It is with these two purposes in mind that the Tathāgata has prescribed the "covering over as with grass" for his disciples.
Out of compassion for householders and to cut off the faction of those with evil desires—
it was for these two reasons that the Tathāgata established the "covering over as with grass" for his disciples.
It was for these two reasons that the Tathāgata established the "covering over as with grass" for his disciples.
For the purpose of inspiring confidence in those without it, and for the further increase of confidence in those who already have it—
it is with these two benefits in mind that the Tathāgata has prescribed the "covering over as with grass" for his disciples.
It is with two benefits in mind that the Tathāgata has prescribed the "covering over as with grass" for his disciples.
For the endurance of the true Dhamma and for the support of the Vinaya—
it was with these two purposes in mind that the Tathāgata prescribed the "covering over as with grass" for his disciples.
The fourth chapter, on what was not previously prescribed, is concluded.
5. The Chapter on the Nine Compendiums (Navasaṅgahavagga):

The nine compendiums are—the compendium of bases (vatthu), the compendium of failures (vipatti), the compendium of offenses (āpatti), the compendium of origins (nidāna), the compendium of persons (puggala), the compendium of aggregates (khandha), the compendium of origins (samuṭṭhāna), the compendium of legal issues (adhikaraṇa), and the compendium of principles for settling disputes (samatha).
When a legal case has arisen, if both the plaintiff and the defendant arrive, the grounds of the case must be reported to both.
Having had the grounds of the case reported to both, the statements of both must be heard.
Having heard the statements of both, both should be addressed as follows:
“If you say, ‘When this legal issue of ours has been settled, both of us will be satisfied,’ then that legal issue should be accepted by the Saṅgha.
If they say,
“Both of us will be satisfied,” the Saṅgha should accept that legal issue.
If the assembly is full of shamelessness, it should be settled by a committee.
If the assembly is full of ignorance, a master of the Vinaya should be sought, by whose Dhamma, by whose Vinaya, and by whose Teacher’s instruction that legal issue is settled;
in that manner should that legal issue be settled.
The basis must be known; the clan must be known; the name must be known; the offense must be known.
"Sexual intercourse" is both the basis and the clan;
"an offense entailing defeat" is both the name and the offense.
“Taking what is not given” (adinnādāna) is both the object and the category;
“an offense entailing expulsion” (pārājika) is both the name and the offense.
“A human being” (manussaviggaha) is both the object and the category.
"Pārājika" is both a name and an offense.
"Superhuman state" (uttarimanussadhamma) is both the basis and the category—
thus, "pārājika" is both a name and an offense.
"Emitting semen" refers both to the objective basis and the category;
it is both the name "Saṅghādisesa" and the offense itself.
"Physical contact" refers both to the objective basis and the category.
“Saṅghādisesa” is both a name and an offense.
“Vulgar speech” is both the subject matter and the category—
“saṅghādisesa” is both a name and an offense.
"Attakāmā" (one who desires for herself) is both the basis and the category;
"saṅghādisesa" is both the name and the offense.
"Sañcaritta" (mediating between men and women) is both the basis and the category.
“Saṅghādisesa” is both a name and an offense.
“Having a hut built by means of begging” is both the subject matter and the category—
“saṅghādisesa” is both a name and an offense.
"Causing a large dwelling to be built": both the site and the undertaking—this is both the name "Saṅghādisesa" and the offense itself.
"Groundlessly charging a bhikkhu with an offense entailing defeat": both the basis and the undertaking—this is both the name "Saṅghādisesa" and the offense itself.
“Saṅghādisesa” is both a name and an offense.

To accuse a bhikkhu of an offense entailing defeat (pārājika) by taking some part or mere semblance of a legal issue belonging to a different category is both the basis and the character [of the offense]—
it is both a name and an offense called “saṅghādisesa.”
For a monk who causes a schism in the Saṅgha, the failure to desist after being admonished up to three times constitutes both the basis and the category for what is called a *saṅghādisesa*—
namely, both the name and the offense.
For the monks who side with the schismatic, the failure to desist after being admonished up to three times constitutes both the basis and the category [for the offense].
“Saṅghādisesa” is both a name and an offense.
For a monk who is difficult to speak with, the failure to desist after being admonished up to three times is both the basis and the category—
it is both a name and an offense called “saṅghādisesa.”
For a monk who corrupts families, the failure to desist after being admonished up to three times: this is both the basis and the category;

it is called a *saṅghādisesa*, which is both a name and an offense… [as before] … With respect to disrespect, the voiding of feces, urine, or spittle into water: this is both the basis and the category.
*Dukkaṭa* means both a name and an offense.
The fifth chapter, the Section on the Ninefold Group, is finished.
Its summary verse:
The motion for announcement and the motion itself,
with the second [announcement] and the fourth;
the matter, the motion, and the proclamation.
And the delimitation of the boundary.
Resolution in the presence of the accused, resolution by questioning,
and resolution by admission are worthy of the Vinaya.
The matter, the Saṅgha, and the individual;
the motion, not after the motion, and the motion itself.
The matter, the Saṅgha, and the individual.
At the wrong time,
and too small or too large,
with broken shadows, and with signs.
It breaks through rivers, the ocean, and natural lakes;
it overflows the boundaries.
Groups of four and five;
groups of ten and twenty;
those not brought forward and those brought forward.
Persons who have reached the stage of formal acts, those entitled to a motion,
and those entitled to a formal act; the five grounds for a formal announcement.
The motion (*ñatti*) has nine bases;
the motion followed by one proclamation (*ñattidutiya*) has seven bases,
and that with three proclamations (*ñatticatuttha*) has seven bases.
Great comfort and ill-will,
the virtuous and the taints;
enmity, fault, and fear—
Unwholesome for householders,
evil desires for those without faith,
and the establishment of the Dhamma for those with faith.
Through assistance with the Vinaya,
through the recitation of the Pātimokkha,
and through the suspension of the Pātimokkha.
The invitation ceremony and its suspension;
censure, demotion,
banishment, and reconciliation.
Suspension, probation,
the beginning, penance, and rehabilitation;
reinstatement, and banishment.
The same applies to full ordination (upasampadā):
the motion for notification, the motion with one proclamation, and the motion with three proclamations.
What was not laid down was laid down;
presence is for face-to-face settlement;
absence of delusion and majority decision.
The "covering over as with grass" is for the worse;
it concerns the failure of the matter, the offense,
the origin, and the person.
The aggregates and their origins,
the legal issues and the means of settlement, as well as the summaries.
Thus ends the section on names and offenses.
The Parivāra is finished.
The Parivāra-pāḷi is finished.
The concluding verses:
Having inquired here and there about the path of the Buddha’s teaching, and...
The one named Dīpanāma, of great wisdom,
a retainer of what has been heard and discerning,
[composed] this summary of the detailed exposition.
Having reflected upon it in the middle watch of the night,
he had it written down for the benefit and ease of his disciples.
Regarding what was stated as "the parivāra," all of it—
both the subject matter and its characteristics—
is for the sake of the meaning within the True Dhamma by means of the meaning.
He protected the Dhamma as it was established by the Dhamma,
just as the ocean protects Jambudīpa.
Not knowing the *parivāra*, how could there be a determination of the Dhamma? [The categories are:
failure, basis, and formulation.
The supplementary rule concerns the person;
it pertains to the designation of the world from both sides and from the perspective of fault.
For one in whom doubt arises,
it is severed by a retinue,
just as a wheel-turning monarch with his great army.
Like a lion in the midst of deer,
like the sun surrounded by its rays,
or like the moon among the hosts of stars.
Just as Brahmā stands before his assembly,
the leader in the midst of the host,
so too is the True Dharma and Discipline.
"One shines by means of one's retinue."
